title: The Rose and the Ring; or, The History of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo. A Fire-Side Pantomime for Great and Small Children
alternative_titles: Rose and the Ring; or, The History of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo. A Fire-Side Pantomime for Great and Small Children
description: Published in December 1854 (title page 1855), written for the Christmas pantomime and for the children of the household: a burlesque fairy tale of two rival kingdoms, the magic rose and ring that make their bearers irresistible, and a cast of comic courtiers.
plot_or_argument: Prince Giglio of Paflagonia and Prince Bulbo of Crim Tartary are both endowed with supernatural charms by the fairy Blackstick; their rivalry for the Princess Angelica, the interference of the wicked Countess Gruffanuff, and the eventual pairing of the true lovers produce a plot of transformations and reversals in which nobody is quite what they seem.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
principal_characters: Prince Giglio of Paflagonia; Prince Bulbo of Crim Tartary; Princess Angelica; Rosalba, the lost Queen of Crim Tartary (Betsinda); the Fairy Blackstick; Countess Gruffanuff; King Valoroso XXIV; King Padella; Glumboso; Captain Hedzoff
literary_form: Children's fantasy (illustrated by the author)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is retrospective narration and the extended aside.
historical_context: The Victorian pantomime and the Christmas gift book, the chapbook and fairy-tale revival of the 1840s-50s, and the new market for children's illustrated books that Thackeray, Dickens and Ruskin all entered.
literary_significance: The Rose and the Ring is one of the two or three founding texts of Victorian children's fantasy and the direct precursor of the comic fairy tale from Thackeray to Nesbit and beyond; its subversive treatment of royal and parental authority is unusual for its decade and it remains one of the funniest children's books of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as W. M. Thackeray. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1855, as children's fantasy (illustrated by the author), by William Makepeace Thackeray. Composed in None. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography
description: Published on 16 October 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell, and the novel that changed the position of the first-person heroine in English fiction: an autobiography of a plain, poor, passionate woman who insists on speaking in her own voice.
plot_or_argument: Jane Eyre, orphaned and abused at Gateshead by her aunt Mrs Reed, is sent to Lowood school, where she survives the regime of Mr Brocklehurst and the death of her friend Helen Burns. She becomes governess at Thornfield Hall, falls in love with her employer Edward Rochester, and on their wedding day discovers his mad wife Bertha Mason, kept in the attic. She flees, is taken in by the Rivers family, inherits a fortune from her uncle, refuses St John Rivers's proposal of a missionary marriage, and returns to find Rochester blinded and maimed by the fire that killed Bertha, to marry him as an equal.
narrative_structure: First-person retrospective autobiography in three volumes, each organised around a household (Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Marsh End, Ferndean) and each ending in expulsion or flight.
principal_characters: Jane Eyre; Edward Fairfax Rochester; Bertha Mason; Mrs Reed; Mr Brocklehurst; Helen Burns; Miss Temple; St John Rivers; Diana and Mary Rivers; Adèle Varens; Grace Poole; Blanche Ingram
literary_form: Novel in three volumes, first person ('edited by Currer Bell')
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s: the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, the governess's anomalous class position, the colonial fortune of the West Indies (Bertha Mason's family and Rochester's Jamaican estate), and the legal doctrine of coverture that made a wife's property her husband's.
literary_significance: Jane Eyre is the founding text of the English feminist novel and one of the two or three most influential novels in the language; its first-person heroine who claims the right to feel, its treatment of colonial wealth at the centre of the English house, and its Gothic machinery inside a realist frame have made it a permanent subject of criticism, from the Brontës' contemporaries to Gilbert and Gubar's madwoman and Spivak's postcolonial reading.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Smith, Elder of London on 16 October 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell; the second edition of January 1848 carries the author's preface and the dedication to Thackeray. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Shirley: A Tale
description: Published in October 1849, written during the illness and deaths of Emily and Anne, and set in the Luddite Yorkshire of 1811-12: the first English novel to make an industrial dispute its central public subject, and the one in which Brontë tried to write a social novel on the scale of her contemporaries.
plot_or_argument: Robert Gérard Moore, a mill-owner of Belgian descent, attempts to introduce machinery into his mill during the Napoleonic blockade and is attacked by the Luddite frame-breakers; his mill is defended by troops. His cousin Caroline Helstone, neglected by her family, falls ill, and Shirley Keeldar, the heiress who gives the novel its name, takes up Caroline's cause. Shirley at last accepts Robert's brother Louis Moore, the tutor who has loved her in silence, and Caroline, who discovers that the quiet Mrs Pryor is her own mother, is united with Robert when the repeal of the Orders in Council restores the mill's prosperity.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
principal_characters: Shirley Keeldar; Caroline Helstone; Robert Gérard Moore; Louis Moore; the Reverend Matthewson Helstone; Mrs Pryor, Caroline's mother; Hortense Moore; Hiram Yorke; Joe Scott; William Farren; the curates Malone, Donne and Sweeting
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; industrial
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
historical_context: The Luddite risings of 1811-12 and the Yorkshire frame-breaking, the Napoleonic Orders in Council and the blockade, and the Chartist and 1848 revolutionary year in which Brontë was writing. The record dates the work as composed between 1848 and 1849 and first published in 1849 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Shirley is one of the earliest English novels to give the industrial conflict serious fictional treatment, and its two heroines — the heiress who owns the mill property and the penniless relation who must work — set out the 'woman question' of the 1840s in terms that the 1850s debate over 'surplus women' took up. It is also the only Brontë novel with a sustained comic and social panorama.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in October 1849 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Villette
description: Published in three volumes in January 1853, and the most inward and formally controlled of Charlotte Brontë's novels: the story of Lucy Snowe in a French-speaking girls' school in the invented city of Villette, drawn from the Pensionnat Heger in Brussels.
plot_or_argument: Lucy Snowe, without family or money, goes to Villette as a teacher and then as a schoolmistress, loves the autocratic Paul Emanuel, and is separated from him by his voyage to the West Indies; the novel also contains the ghostly visit of the nun and the subplot of the heiress Polly Home and Dr John Bretton. The ending leaves Paul's fate uncertain, with a report of a storm and a shipwreck.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Lucy Snowe (the narrator); M. Paul Emanuel; Dr John Graham Bretton; Paulina Mary Home de Bassompierre (Polly); Ginevra Fanshawe; Madame Beck; Mrs Bretton; Count de Hamal; Miss Marchmont
literary_form: Novel in three volumes, first person
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
historical_context: The Brussels pensionnat, the English governess abroad, the Catholic-Protestant antagonism of continental and English manners, and the debate over women's employment that followed the 1851 census. The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Villette is now generally read as Brontë's finest novel and one of the great novels of interiority in English; its refusal of a closed happy ending and its study of repression and vocation made it central to twentieth-century feminist criticism, and its analysis of a woman's professional identity anticipates the New Woman fiction of the 1890s.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in January 1853 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Professor
description: Charlotte Brontë's first novel, written in 1846 and rejected by every publisher to whom it was offered; it was published posthumously in 1857 with a preface by her widower, Arthur Bell Nicholls. It is a prose fiction work of 1857 by Charlotte Brontë; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: William Crimsworth, an orphan without connections, rejects the patronage of his Yorkshire brother and goes to Brussels, where he teaches at a boys' school and then at Mademoiselle Reuter's girls' school; he falls in love with Frances Henri, a Swiss-English pupil-teacher, marries her, and returns to England to run a school of their own.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: William Crimsworth (the narrator); Frances Evans Henri; Zoraïde Reuter; M. Pelet; Edward Crimsworth; Yorke Hunsden; Victor Crimsworth
literary_form: Novel in two volumes (posthumous)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The author's characteristic manner is intense first-person narration, often retrospective and addressed to an unnamed reader.
historical_context: The Brussels of the 1840s, the position of the English master abroad, and the professional ambition of a self-made man of letters — the novel's subject is the one that Brontë knew from Heger. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1857 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Professor anticipates Villette and is a key document for the study of Brontë's development: its plain, unromantic hero, its refusal of the love-plot's conventional hierarchy and its insistence on work as the basis of self-respect make it the first Brontë statement of the themes she later transformed.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Currer Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Charlotte Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Refused by seven publishers during the author's lifetime and issued posthumously by Smith, Elder in June 1857 with a notice by Elizabeth Gaskell. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Wuthering Heights
description: Published in December 1847 in three volumes together with Anne Brontë's Agnes Grey, under the pseudonym Ellis Bell, and the one Victorian novel that has never been domesticated into the conventions of its decade: a chronicle of two families on the Yorkshire moors, told by two partial narrators, in which the passion between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff exceeds every social and religious form available to it.
plot_or_argument: Mr Lockwood, the tenant of Thrushcross Grange, visits his landlord Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights and is told the history of the house by the servant Nelly Dean. The foundling Heathcliff, brought home from Liverpool by Mr Earnshaw, and Catherine Earnshaw grow up inseparable on the moors; Catherine marries Edgar Linton for social position, Heathcliff returns wealthy and embittered, and the second half of the novel follows his revenge on the next generation — Hindley's son Hareton, and Catherine's daughter Cathy, whom he forces to marry his dying son Linton — until his own death releases the pair into their marriage and the ghosts of the first Catherine and Heathcliff are reported on the moor.
narrative_structure: Two framed narratives (Lockwood's outer frame and Nelly Dean's inner chronicle) covering two generations over some thirty years, with a symmetrical doubling of the first and second pairs of lovers.
principal_characters: Heathcliff; Catherine Earnshaw; Catherine Linton; Edgar Linton; Isabella Linton; Hindley Earnshaw; Hareton Earnshaw; Cathy Linton; Linton Heathcliff; Nelly Dean; Joseph; Mr Lockwood; Mr Earnshaw; Zillah
literary_form: Novel in three volumes (with Agnes Grey), framed narrative
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is a frame-within-a-frame narrative with two partial and unreliable narrators.
historical_context: The West Riding of Yorkshire in the 1770s-1802, the yeoman and gentry economy of the moorland farms, the Liverpool of the slave trade and the Irish famine emigration (the source of Heathcliff's origin, which the novel leaves unexplained), and the Calvinist and Methodist religious culture of the Brontë household.
literary_significance: Wuthering Heights is the most radical novel of the Victorian period and the only one that has resisted every attempt to place it in a history of the novel's development: its double narration, its two-generation structure and its unassimilable passion made it a permanent test case for criticism (from Charlotte Brontë's 1850 preface to Kermode, Miller, Gilbert and Gubar, and the postcolonial reading of Heathcliff's racial origin). Its influence runs through the modern Gothic, the novel of the moors, and the fiction of the American South.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Ellis Bell, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Emily Brontë is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Thomas Cautley Newby in December 1847, dated 1848, as Ellis Bell, the first two volumes holding Wuthering Heights and the third Agnes Grey; the second edition of 1850 carries the editor's biographical notice by the surviving sister. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Gondal Poems
description: The body of verse written by Emily (and, in part, Anne) Brontë from about 1836 into the 1840s, set in the imaginary island kingdom of Gondal in the North Pacific and concerned with its queens, its prisoners and its wars; a substantial part of it was printed in the 1846 volume, and the prose chronicles that framed it were lost.
plot_or_argument: The poems are dramatic fragments rather than a continuous narrative: 'A. G. Rochelle' is a prisoner's song of endurance, 'The Death of A. G. Rochelle' and the Queen Augusta poems dramatise the politics of Gondal, and the elegiac and love poems register the passions of its royal houses. The recovering of the Gondal story from the poems has been a long scholarly exercise.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
literary_form: Poems of a private imaginary chronicle
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The author's characteristic manner is a frame-within-a-frame narrative with two partial and unreliable narrators.
historical_context: A childhood and adolescent imaginative project shared with Anne Brontë from 1827 onwards, descended from the Brontës' reading of Scott, Byron and Blackwood's, and conducted in manuscript notebooks (the 'Gondal poems' are preserved in the Ashley and Bonnell collections).
literary_significance: The Gondal poems are the private laboratory of Emily Brontë's art and a central document for the study of the imaginative life of the Brontë household; they are the clearest English example of a nineteenth-century writer maintaining a complete secondary world across two decades.
attribution_notes: The attribution of individual Gondal poems between Emily and Anne Brontë rests on manuscript evidence and on Charlotte's 1850 editing; a number remain uncertain, and the prose chronicles are lost.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1846, as poems of a private imaginary chronicle, by Emily Brontë. Composed between 1836 and 1848. The title is also recorded as The Gondal Poems. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Agnes Grey
description: Published in December 1847 with Wuthering Heights, under the pseudonym Acton Bell, and the first English novel to describe the governess's working life from inside, without either the Gothic or the sentimental softening that the theme received from her sisters.
plot_or_argument: Agnes Grey, the daughter of a poor clergyman, takes a post with the Bloomfield family and then with the Murrays, and the novel records in close detail the humiliations of her position, the indiscipline of her charges and the indifference of their parents. She falls in love with the curate Edward Weston, is separated from him, and is reunited when her family's circumstances change and he seeks her out.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Agnes Grey; Edward Weston; Mrs Bloomfield; Mr Bloomfield; the Bloomfield children; Mrs Murray; Rosalie Murray; Matilda Murray; Mr Grey; Mrs Grey; Nancy Brown
literary_form: Novel in three volumes (with Wuthering Heights), first person
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text.
historical_context: The governess question of the 1830s-40s, the Clergy Daughters' School and the private academy, and the market for educated women's labour that the 1851 census later quantified. The record dates the work as composed between 1845 and 1846 and first published in 1847 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Agnes Grey is the indispensable English novel of the governess and one of the most exact accounts of women's paid work in the nineteenth century; its plainness was read as weakness by Victorian reviewers and is now read as its formal principle, and it stands with Gaskell's Ruth and Brontë's Villette in the pre-feminist analysis of women's economic position.
attribution_notes: Published under the pseudonym Acton Bell; the authorship was established with the other 'Bell' novels in 1848, and Charlotte Brontë's 1850 reissue carried a biographical notice.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Thomas Cautley Newby in December 1847 as Acton Bell in the third volume with Wuthering Heights, and separately in a second edition in July 1850. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
description: Published in three volumes in June 1848 under the pseudonym Acton Bell, and the most controversial of the Brontë novels in its own time: the story of a wife who leaves a violent and alcoholic husband and supports herself and her child by her own work, told through letters and a journal.
plot_or_argument: Gilbert Markham, a Yorkshire farmer, falls in love with Helen Graham, a widow newly arrived at Wildfell Hall, and discovers through her journal that she is in fact the wife of Arthur Huntingdon, whom she married against advice and who has become a drunkard and an adulterer. Helen has left him and taken their son; after Huntingdon's death she is free to marry Gilbert, and the novel closes with their union and the recovery of the estate.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Helen Graham (Helen Huntingdon); Gilbert Markham; Arthur Huntingdon; Frederick Lawrence; Mrs Markham; Rose Markham; Annabella Lowborough; Lord Lowborough; Ralph Hattersley; Milicent Hargrave; Rachel
literary_form: Novel in three volumes, epistolary and framed first person
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence.
historical_context: The 1820s-30s and the law of coverture, the custody of children as a husband's property, the temperance agitation of the 1830s, and the contemporary debate on the 'social evil' of drink and prostitution.
literary_significance: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall is the first English novel to defend a wife's right to leave an abusive husband, and its unsparing treatment of alcoholism and marital cruelty made it the most attacked book of the Brontës in 1848 and the most valued by modern feminist criticism. Its formal design — a journal inside letters inside a first-person narrative — is the most experimental structure among the Brontë novels.
attribution_notes: Published under the pseudonym Acton Bell; the novel's frankness about marital cruelty drew attacks on the 'coarseness' of the Bell novels, and Charlotte Brontë's 1850 judgement that it was 'hardly ... desirable' shaped its neglect until the twentieth century.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Thomas Cautley Newby in June 1848 as Acton Bell; the second edition of 1848 carries the author's preface answering its reviewers. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Scenes of Clerical Life
description: Three tales — 'The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton', 'Mr Gilfil's Love-Story' and 'Janet's Repentance' — published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1857 and collected in 1858: the first fiction of George Eliot, written when she was already the author of translations and the editor of the Westminster Review.
plot_or_argument: 'Amos Barton' follows the failure and death of a dull curate's wife in the parish of Shepperton; 'Mr Gilfil's Love-Story' recovers the tragic past of the old vicar of Knebley; 'Janet's Repentance' traces the conversion of a drunken wife-beating clergyman's wife in the town of Milby through the ministry of the Evangelical Mr Tryan.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Amos Barton; Milly Barton; Mr Gilfil; Caterina Sarti; Janet Dempster; Mr Tryan; Mr Dempster
literary_form: Three linked tales (Blackwood's Magazine, 1857); two volumes 1858
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The Warwickshire and Staffordshire of the 1820s-30s, the Evangelical revival inside the Church of England, and the provincial town of the pre-Reform era; the stories were modelled on the recollections of Eliot's aunt, Elizabeth Tomlinson.
literary_significance: Scenes of Clerical Life introduced the fictional method that Eliot developed for the next twenty years — the provincial community studied through several ordinary lives, the sympathy that refuses moral simplification, and the narrator who speaks as a member of the community — and it established her as the most serious new novelist of the 1850s.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: The three tales ran in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from January to November 1857 and were published in two volumes by William Blackwood in May 1858. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Adam Bede
description: Published in three volumes in February 1859 and an immediate popular success: a novel of rural Warwickshire in 1799, and the book in which Eliot's realism is stated most programmatically — 'a faithful account of men and things as they have mirrored themselves in my mind'.
plot_or_argument: Adam Bede, a carpenter, loves the vain dairy-maid Hetty Sorrel, who is seduced by the young squire Arthur Donnithorne; when Hetty discovers she is pregnant she sets out to find Arthur, gives birth on the road, and is convicted of the murder of her child. Adam marries the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris after Hetty's reprieve and transportation, and the novel ends with the community restored and the past understood.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Adam Bede; Dinah Morris; Hetty Sorrel; Arthur Donnithorne; Seth Bede; Lisbeth Bede; Martin Poyser; Mrs Poyser; Bartle Massey; the Squire; Molly
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The rural Midlands of 1799 and the Napoleonic wars, the Methodist revival of the 1790s and the preaching of women like Dinah, and the agrarian society of the estate and the farm. The record dates the work as composed in 1858 and first published in 1859 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet; Pre-Raphaelitism and the Truth to Nature, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; industrial and condition-of-england novel.
literary_significance: Adam Bede made Eliot famous and set the standard for the English regional novel of the next half-century; its sympathetic treatment of a Methodist woman preacher and its refusal to punish Hetty with a simple death made it a model for the serious treatment of ordinary lives, and its 'realism' became the term of the debate about the purpose of fiction in the 1860s.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by William Blackwood in February 1859; the authorship was an open secret from July 1859. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Mill on the Floss
description: Published in April 1860, the most autobiographical of Eliot's novels and the one that states her central subject: the conflict between a woman's need for intellectual life and the claims of family loyalty, set on the river Floss in the Lincolnshire of the 1820s-30s.
plot_or_argument: Maggie Tulliver, passionate and clever, grows up in the mill of Dorlcote against the preference of her family for her prosaic brother Tom; the family is ruined by the lawsuit of the lawyer Wakem, Maggie meets Wakem's hunchback son Philip in secret, is compromised by her cousin's fiancé Stephen Guest, and is finally reconciled with Tom in the flood that drowns them both in each other's arms.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Maggie Tulliver; Tom Tulliver; Mr Tulliver; Mrs Tulliver; Philip Wakem; Stephen Guest; Lucy Deane; Lawyer Wakem; Bob Jakin; aunt Glegg; aunt Pullet
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; novel of development
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The 1820s-30s, the mill and the river trade of St Ogg's, the education available to clever girls, and the legal costs of the Chancery suit that ruins the Tullivers. The record dates the work as composed between 1859 and 1860 and first published in 1860 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: The Mill on the Floss is the great English novel of a girl's education and the fullest early statement of the problem of the intellectual woman; its ending has been the central test case in criticism of Eliot's realism, and it is the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century novel of female development.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by William Blackwood of Edinburgh and London in April 1860. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe
description: Published in one volume in April 1861, Eliot's shortest novel and the one most often read as a parable: the story of a linen-weaver who loses his faith and his gold and is restored by the child who walks into his cottage.
plot_or_argument: Silas Marner, falsely accused of theft by his fellow Dissenters at Lantern Yard, settles in the village of Raveloe, where he hoards his guineas until they are stolen by the squire's son Dunstan Cass. A little girl, Eppie, comes to his fire one winter night, and the novel follows her upbringing and the attempt of her true father Godfrey Cass to reclaim her, which she refuses in favour of the weaver who raised her.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Silas Marner; Eppie; Godfrey Cass; Dunstan Cass; Nancy Lammeter; Squire Cass; Dolly Winthrop; William Dane; Molly Farren
literary_form: Novel in one volume; realist novel of common life
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The rural Midlands at the turn of the nineteenth century, the Dissenting chapel and the village church, the isolation of the weaver and the new industrial economy, and the paternalism of the squire's family.
literary_significance: Silas Marner is the most formally perfect of Eliot's novels and the one that most clearly states her secular religion of sympathy; it is a permanent school text and the standard English example of the redemptive foundling plot, and its treatment of religious community and of the alienated craftsman anticipates the sociology of the novel in the twentieth century.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in two volumes by William Blackwood in April 1861. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Romola
description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from July 1862 to August 1863 and published in three volumes: Eliot's only historical novel, a study of Florence in the years of Savonarola (1492-98) and the most ambitious attempt by a Victorian novelist to reconstruct the Renaissance mind.
plot_or_argument: Romola de' Bardi, the daughter of a blind classical scholar, marries the Greek adventurer Tito Melema, who betrays her father, her brother and her city; the novel follows her through the expulsion of the Medici, the preaching of Savonarola and the plague, her flight from Florence, and her return to a life of charity in the household of the Platonist Bardo.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Romola de' Bardi; Tito Melema; Savonarola; Bardo de' Bardi; Baldassarre; Tessa; Nello; Piero di Cosimo; Bernardo del Nero; Dino
literary_form: Historical novel (Cornhill Magazine, 1862-63); three volumes 1863
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The Florence of Lorenzo de' Medici, the French invasion of 1494, Savonarola's republic and his execution in 1498, and the Victorian vogue for the Italian Renaissance that produced Browning's poems and Ruskin's and Pater's criticism in the same years.
literary_significance: Romola is the most scholarly of Victorian historical novels and the fullest English attempt to imagine the Renaissance from within its own intellectual life; it is also the key text for the Victorian debate about the relation of art to moral duty, and its heroine is one of the few fully realised women intellectuals in Victorian fiction.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in The Cornhill Magazine from July 1862 to August 1863, where the author was paid £10,000 for the serial rights, and published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in July 1863. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Felix Holt, the Radical
description: Published in 1866, set in the Midlands at the time of the first Reform Bill (1832), and the novel in which Eliot confronted electoral politics most directly: a study of radicalism, inheritance and class loyalty in the town of Treby Magna.
plot_or_argument: Felix Holt, a watchmaker and Radical, and Harold Transome, the heir of Transome Court who returns from the East to stand as a Radical, are rivals for the hand of Esther Lyon, who is revealed to be the true heir of the Transome estate; the election riot, the trial of Felix for manslaughter, and the family secret of the Transome inheritance resolve into Esther's renunciation of her claim and her marriage to Felix.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
principal_characters: Felix Holt; Esther Lyon; Harold Transome; Mrs Transome; Rufus Lyon; Matthew Jermyn; Sir Maximus Debarry; Christian; Tommy Trounsem
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; industrial
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The General Election of 1832 and the Reform Act, the decline of the landed estate, the money of the East India trade, and the religious Dissent of the provincial town. The record dates the work as composed between 1865 and 1866 and first published in 1866 and the corpus places it within Chartism and the Condition-of-England Novel; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under industrial and condition-of-england novel; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Felix Holt is the most direct Victorian novel about parliamentary reform and the most serious attempt by a major novelist to represent working-class political conviction; its analysis of the transference of estates and of the rhetoric of the hustings is a valuable document for the social history of 1832, and its heroine's choice is one of Eliot's most carefully argued moral conclusions.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by William Blackwood in June 1866. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life
description: Published in eight parts from December 1871 to December 1872, set in the provincial town of Middlemarch in the years of the first Reform Bill, and generally regarded as the greatest of Victorian novels: a study of four intersecting lives in a community, constructed on the principle that no single centre of consciousness can see the whole.
plot_or_argument: Dorothea Brooke marries the pedantic scholar Edward Casaubon in the hope of sharing a great work, and is widowed into freedom and a second marriage with Will Ladislaw; the young doctor Tertius Lydgate comes to Middlemarch with plans for hospital reform and a new pathology, marries the beautiful and expensive Rosamond Vincy, and is destroyed by debt and provincial opinion; the banker Bulstrode's buried past returns to ruin him; and Fred Vincy is saved by Mary Garth's refusal to marry a man without a vocation.
narrative_structure: Four interwoven plots across eight monthly parts, with a Prelude and a Finale and a narration that moves freely among the consciousnesses of the town.
principal_characters: Dorothea Brooke; Edward Casaubon; Will Ladislaw; Tertius Lydgate; Rosamond Vincy; Nicholas Bulstrode; Fred Vincy; Mary Garth; Caleb Garth; Mr Brooke; Celia Brooke; Sir James Chettam; Peter Featherstone; Mr Farebrother; John Raffles
literary_form: Novel in eight monthly parts (1871-72); four volumes 1872
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The late 1820s and the first Reform Bill, the new medical science of the 1820s, the coming of the railway to the Midlands, the death of George IV and the hopes of reform, and the provincial town's government by the 'Middlemarch' oligarchy of the landowning and professional families.
literary_significance: Middlemarch is the central novel of the English nineteenth century: it brought the multiplot novel to its highest point, made the study of ordinary lives an instrument of moral philosophy, and produced the period's most quoted statement of the ethics of sympathy ('the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts'). Its influence on the modern novel of consciousness and on the criticism of realism has been continuous since its publication.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by William Blackwood in eight bi-monthly parts from December 1871 to December 1872, and in four volumes between 1872 and 1873; the full title is Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Daniel Deronda
description: Published in eight parts from February 1874 to September 1876, and the last completed novel: a double plot that sets the English marriage market and gentry society against the discovery of a Jewish national destiny, and the first English novel to take Zionism seriously as a political idea.
plot_or_argument: Gwendolen Harleth, beautiful and self-willed, marries the sadistic Grandcourt to save her family from ruin and is drawn to Daniel Deronda, who rescues Mirah Lapidoth from drowning. Deronda discovers that he is Jewish, the ward of Sir Hugo Mallinger and the heir of a Jewish scholar's teaching, and the novel ends with his marriage to Mirah, his departure for the East, and Gwendolen's letter left unread.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Daniel Deronda; Gwendolen Harleth; Henleigh Grandcourt; Mirah Lapidoth; Mordecai; Sir Hugo Mallinger; the Princess Halm-Eberstein; Mrs Davilow; Hans Meyrick; Ezra Cohen; Klesmer
literary_form: Novel in eight monthly parts (1874-76); four volumes 1876
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The 1860s-70s: the Jewish community of London and the new political Zionism of Moses Hess and the pre-Herzlian national movement, the gambling spa of Leubronn, the English country house, and the aestheticism of the 1870s.
literary_significance: Daniel Deronda is the most ambitious of Eliot's novels and the most contested: its Jewish plot made it the object of criticism from Henry James to the modern postcolonial and Jewish studies, and it is a fundamental text for the history of literary Zionism and of English representations of Jewish identity. Its Gwendolen plot is one of the great studies of a woman's moral education through terror.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by William Blackwood in eight monthly parts from February to September 1876 and in four volumes in September 1876. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Impressions of Theophrastus Such
description: Published in 1879, the last book Eliot published in her lifetime: eighteen essays and character sketches written in the person of Theophrastus Such, a bachelor of independent means, on vanity, on the Jewish intellect, on the 'modern Hep! Hep! Hep!', on authorship and on the moral life.
plot_or_argument: There is no continuous narrative: the essays are the observations of a fictional essayist on his contemporaries, and the volume's interest is in the construction of the persona — a dry, self-aware, slightly ridiculous man — and in the essay on the Jews that anticipates the themes of Daniel Deronda.
narrative_structure: A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
principal_characters: Theophrastus Such, the essayist-narrator; the contemporaries he anatomises — Merman, Lentulus, Hinze, Touchwood, Spike, Mordax, Mixtus, Euphorion and Vorticella
literary_form: Essays in the person of a fictional essayist
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is aphoristic and digressive narration that addresses the reader as a moral equal.
historical_context: The 1870s, the periodical culture of the Fortnightly and the Nineteenth Century, the debate on Jewish emancipation, and the late-Victorian taste for the essayistic persona. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1879 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Impressions of Theophrastus Such is Eliot's most formally experimental book and an important document in the Victorian essay tradition; it is now read as a significant contribution to the debate on Jewish identity and to the history of the fictional essayist, and it is the last word of the century's most intellectually ambitious novelist.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name George Eliot, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to George Eliot is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1879, as essays in the person of a fictional essayist, by George Eliot. Composed in None. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Mary Barton: A Tale of Manchester Life
description: Published anonymously in October 1848, and the first English novel to take the Manchester mill-worker's household as its subject: written after the death of Gaskell's infant son and after years of parish visiting among the poor of Manchester.
plot_or_argument: John Barton, a mill-hand and Chartist, and his daughter Mary live through the trade depression of the late 1830s and the Chartist petition of 1839; Mary is courted by the mill-owner's son Harry Carson and by the sailor Jem Wilson, and when Carson is murdered John Barton, in his capacity as the union's delegate, is the killer. Mary clears Jem of the charge and her father's confession and death close the novel, which ends with the masters persuaded to listen to the men.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
principal_characters: Mary Barton; John Barton; Jem Wilson; Harry Carson; Margaret Legh; Alice Wilson; Job Legh; Esther; Mr Carson; Will Wilson
literary_form: Novel in two volumes (anonymous)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work was published anonymously or under an initial, and the authorship was established afterwards. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The Manchester cotton industry in the depression of 1837-42, the Chartist petition and the Plug Plot riots of 1842, the new poor law, and the epidemic fever of the 1840s; the novel's account of the Barton household's hunger is drawn from Gaskell's own visiting.
literary_significance: Mary Barton opened the condition-of-England novel and made the industrial poor the subject of serious English fiction for the first time; Dickens, Kingsley, Disraeli and Engels's readership all took note, and the novel is now the founding text of the criticism of Victorian industrial fiction.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1848; the authorship was soon known, and Gaskell's name appeared on the title page of the second edition.
bibliographical_notes: Published anonymously in two volumes by Chapman and Hall in October 1848; the full title is Mary Barton: A Tale of Manchester Life. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Cranford
description: Serialised in Household Words from December 1851 to May 1853 and published in one volume: the comic idyll of a Cheshire town of 'Amazons' — widows and spinsters of small means and great dignity — modelled on Knutsford, where Gaskell was brought up.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, Mary Smith, records the economy and etiquette of Cranford: Miss Matty and Miss Deborah Jenkyns, the loss of the family fortune in a bank failure, the return of Miss Matty's brother Peter from India, and a series of small domestic crises handled by the town's unwritten code of gentility. It has no continuous plot and is organised as a sequence of episodes.
narrative_structure: Episodic linked sketches narrated by a visiting witness, in the manner of the eighteenth-century periodical essay rather than of the plotted novel.
principal_characters: Miss Matty Jenkyns; Miss Deborah Jenkyns; Mary Smith; Peter Jenkyns; Miss Pole; Mrs Jamieson; Lady Glenmire; Captain Brown; Mr Holbrook; Martha
literary_form: Linked sketches (Household Words, 1851-53); one volume 1853
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The 1830s-50s and the world of the genteel poor: the half-pay officer's widow, the tea party, the servant economy, and the railway's arrival at the end of the book. The record dates the work as composed between 1851 and 1853 and first published in 1853 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; realist novel of common life.
literary_significance: Cranford is the finest English comic-idyllic fiction of the century and the founding text of the novel of gentlewomen's economy; its treatment of women living without men and without money is a serious social observation under the comedy, and it has remained continuously in print since 1853.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Gaskell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: The sketches ran in Household Words from December 1851 to May 1853 and were published in two volumes by Smith, Elder in June 1853. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Ruth
description: Published in 1853, the year after Cranford, and the most controversial of Gaskell's books: the story of an orphaned milliner's apprentice who is seduced, abandoned and taken in by a Dissenting minister, and who is not punished with the death that the moral convention of the 1850s required.
plot_or_argument: Ruth Hilton, seduced by the wealthy Henry Bellingham, is taken in by the minister Thurstan Benson and his sister Faith, who pass her off as a widow; she becomes a governess and a nurse, refuses Bellingham's later offer of marriage, and dies of fever while nursing the poor of the town, having been publicly exposed by the father of her pupil.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Ruth Hilton; Henry Bellingham; Thurstan Benson; Faith Benson; Mr Benson; Sally; Leonard; Jemima Bradshaw; Mr Bradshaw
literary_form: Novel in three volumes; new woman
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the marriage-question novel: the domestic scene rendered with exact financial and legal detail, the dialogue of negotiation between the sexes, and the closing argument stated in the terms of the period's reform literature. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The 1830s-50s and the treatment of the 'fallen woman': the milliner's shop, the governess's reference, the Dissenting chapel, and the fever hospital; the novel's refusal of the conventional deathbed of the seduced woman was attacked in reviews and defended by Dickens, who published it.
literary_significance: Ruth is one of the founding texts of Victorian feminist argument about sexuality and the double standard. Its refusal to treat its heroine as a 'fallen woman' and its attack on the cruelty of respectable opinion gave the 1850s debate over the Contagious Diseases and the Magdalen houses its most widely read fictional argument.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Gaskell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in January 1853. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: North and South
description: Serialised in Household Words from September 1854 to January 1855 (the last number after Dickens and Gaskell disputed the ending) and published in two volumes: the great novel of the industrial north seen through a southern woman's eyes.
plot_or_argument: Margaret Hale, whose father has left the Church of England over a matter of conscience, moves with her family from the rural south to the cotton town of Milton, where she comes to know the mill-owner John Thornton and the striking workers Nicholas and Bessy Higgins. A strike and a riot, the death of her parents, her inherited wealth, and Thornton's business failure bring the two together in a marriage of mutual respect and of reconciled regions.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters of the industrial town, the mill, the strike and the household described in the vocabulary of the trade, the plot built on the collision of the two nations.
principal_characters: Margaret Hale; John Thornton; Nicholas Higgins; Bessy Higgins; Mr Hale; Mrs Hale; Frederick Hale; Mrs Thornton; Mr Bell; Henry Lennox; Dixon
literary_form: Novel in weekly parts (Household Words); two volumes 1855
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the industrial novel: the documentary description of the mill, the mine, the street and the strike, the dialect of the workers set against the language of the masters, and the plot built on the collision of the two nations. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The 1850s cotton industry and the Preston strike, the master-and-man conflict of the 1840s-50s, the contrast of the rural south and the industrial north, and the disruption of the Oxford Movement and the secessions to Rome.
literary_significance: North and South is the central English novel of the regional and class division of the nation, and its marriage plot is one of the period's most successful attempts to make a social reconciliation come true in the form of a personal one; it is a permanent counterpart to Hard Times, and its heroine is one of the most fully realised women of Victorian fiction.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Mrs Gaskell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in Household Words from September 1854 to January 1855 in twenty weekly parts and published in two volumes by Chapman and Hall in April 1855 with a new preface. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Wives and Daughters: An Every-Day Story
description: Serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866, unfinished at Gaskell's sudden death in November 1865 and published with the editor's note that the last chapter was wanting; the most mature of her novels.
plot_or_argument: Molly Gibson, the motherless daughter of a country doctor, is given a stepmother in the scheming and charming Hyacinth Clare, and a stepsister in Cynthia Kirkpatrick, whose beauty and improvidence complicate Molly's love for the naturalist Roger Hamley. The novel's interests are inheritance, professional vocation, the provincial town and its gossip; the last chapter was to have married Molly to Roger.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Molly Gibson; Mr Gibson; Hyacinth Clare; Cynthia Kirkpatrick; Roger Hamley; Osborne Hamley; Squire Hamley; Lady Harriet Cumnor; Lord Cumnor; Lady Cumnor; Mr Coxe; Mrs Goodenough
literary_form: Novel in monthly parts (Cornhill Magazine); two volumes 1866
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The 1820s-30s in the fictional county of Hollingford, the professional middle class of the country doctor and the landowning gentry of the Hall and the Towers, and the scientific natural history of the 1830s.
literary_significance: Wives and Daughters is generally regarded as Gaskell's masterpiece and the most satisfying English novel of provincial life after Middlemarch; its unfinished condition has made it a permanent case in the study of the Victorian novel's endings, and its portrait of the stepmother is one of the period's most subtle studies of feminine performance.
attribution_notes: Unfinished at the author's death on 12 November 1865; the Cornhill serial and the 1866 volume text break off before the final chapter, and the intended ending is known only from Gaskell's correspondence and the editor's note.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in The Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866 and published in two volumes by Smith, Elder in August 1866 with the final pages supplied by Frederick Greenwood. The research status is partial. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Life of Charlotte Brontë
description: Commissioned by Patrick Brontë and published in March 1857, the first full biography of Charlotte Brontë and the founding work of Victorian literary biography: a book that shaped the image of the Brontës for the next century and one that had to be withdrawn and revised within months of publication.
plot_or_argument: The biography follows Charlotte from Haworth and the Clergy Daughters' School through the Brussels years, the deaths of Branwell, Emily and Anne and the publication of the novels; Gaskell's method is to quote the letters and to build a portrait of the parsonage and the moorland life around them.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Charlotte Brontë; Patrick Brontë, her father; Branwell Brontë; Emily Brontë; Anne Brontë; Ellen Nussey; Constantin Héger; Arthur Bell Nicholls
literary_form: Biography; review essay, first issued in 1857
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is concrete notation of household economy (what a servant earns, what a dress costs, how a fire is laid).
historical_context: The 1850s, the Brontë legend, and the controversies the book provoked: the attack on the Cowan Bridge school, the libel action threatened over the Carus Wilson account, the treatment of Branwell's dissipation, and the second edition of 1857 with corrections.
literary_significance: The Life of Charlotte Brontë established the modern literary biography in England and created the Brontë myth that later scholarship has had to dismantle; its use of letters and domestic detail founded a method that Gaskell's successors, from Forster's Dickens to the modern biographer, have followed.
attribution_notes: Commissioned by Patrick Brontë; the first edition was withdrawn and revised in 1857 after objections from the family and from the Cowley school, and the standard text is the third edition of 1857 with Gaskell's corrections.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1857, as biography, by Elizabeth Gaskell. Composed in None. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Warden
description: Published in 1855, the first of the Barsetshire novels and the book that made Trollope's reputation: the story of a Church of England warden whose income from a medieval charity is attacked in the newspaper press.
plot_or_argument: Septimus Harding, the warden of Hiram's Hospital at Barchester, draws a comfortable income from a bequest intended for twelve poor men; the reformer John Bold brings a suit, and the affair is taken up by the London press and the archdeacon. Harding resigns rather than fight, and the novel ends with his withdrawal to a small curacy and his daughter Eleanor's marriage.
narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length.
principal_characters: Septimus Harding; Archdeacon Grantly; Eleanor Harding; John Bold; Dr Grantly; Bishop Grantly; Mr Quiverful; Tom Towers; John Hiram
literary_form: Novel in one volume (Barsetshire, 1)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of common life: the continuous chaptered narrative, the full reported dialogue, the exact material description of rooms, clothes, money and work, and the slow accumulation of consequence. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is multiple parallel plots in one book, with a slow rotation of attention.
historical_context: The ecclesiastical commissions and the reform of cathedral and charitable endowments in the 1850s, the new power of the press, and the Oxford Movement's aftermath inside the Church of England. The record dates the work as composed between 1854 and 1855 and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within Arnold and the Criticism of Culture; Tractarian Prose and the Oxford Movement, it is catalogued under realist novel of common life; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Warden introduced the Barsetshire series and the Trollope method: the moral question examined from every point of view until the reader's sympathy is distributed rather than focused. It is the first English novel to make the newspaper a character and to understand institutional reform as a competition of narratives.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Anthony Trollope. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1855, as novel in one volume (barsetshire, 1), by Anthony Trollope. Composed between 1854 and 1855. The record grades the work as secondary canon.
